node-1.label: 12-month-old Caucasian boy presented with convulsive seizures lasting 3-4 seconds, characterized by faltering, smirking with withdrawal of head and eyes

node-2.label: At birth, the patient had a blond hair strand, polydactyly of the right hand, and cardiac rhabdomyoma; at four months, depigmented spots appeared on the torso.

node-3.label: First convulsive seizures were noted at 8 months; psychomotor development was normal for age; no family history of similar conditions.

node-4.label: Physical examination revealed no focal neurological symptoms; physical features included blond hair strand, polydactyly of right hand, and depigmented spots on torso.

why.why: Radiologist analysis reports that genetic testing confirms a pathogenic TSC1 mutation and brain MRI reveals subcortical tubers, fulfilling diagnostic criteria for tuberous sclerosis complex. These definitive molecular and imaging findings, combined with the existing syndromic features of cardiac rhabdomyoma, depigmented spots, blond hair strand, and infantile seizures, raise confidence from 0.85 to 0.97. The additional posterior fossa mass with brainstem compression and hydrocephalus is a recognized complication of tuberous sclerosis complex and further supports the diagnosis.

Genetic confirmation of a pathogenic TSC1 mutation and MRI evidence of subcortical tubers provide definitive evidence of tuberous sclerosis complex, making benign idiopathic infantile seizures untenable. The previously noted cardiac rhabdomyoma and depigmented skin lesions already argued against this diagnosis, and the new molecular and imaging findings reduce confidence to 0.02.

The confirmed pathogenic TSC1 mutation and subcortical tubers on brain MRI establish a genetic cause, excluding acquired symptomatic epilepsy. Normal psychomotor development, absence of focal neurological findings, and lack of acquired structural abnormality are consistent with a genetic disorder, and the confirmed tuberous sclerosis complex diagnosis lowers confidence to 0.01.
